Alternatively, Giramondo founder Ivor Indyk described his house receiving two dollars in patronage for every dollar it generated in sales as of 2013, primarily from the University of Western Sydney which covered salaries and infrastructure, and through the Literature Board of the Australia Council subsidizing roughly seven titles per year (Indyk 2013, 125). Economically supported by institutions that viewed Giramondo’s books as beneficial to the symbolic capital of the university and Australian culture more generally, the publisher operated with the economic aim of only needing to break even on their books. It should be noted, though, that the Indyk family appears to have been rich in cultural and social capital. A reflection on Ivor’s brother, Martin Indyk, by childhood friend Bruce Solomon, speaks to the Sydney milieu in which their families grew up: “our crowd was incredibly successful—judges, geniuses, professors, billionaires” (Alhadeff [2024](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR1 "Alhadeff, Vic. 2024. “Few Australians Have Had Such a Large Impact on the World.” The Jewish Independent, August 26.   
                  https://thejewishindependent.com.au/few-australians-have-had-such-a-large-impact-on-the-world  
                    
                .")). These small presses, in other words, align with Bourdieu’s model for cultural production at the restricted pole, appearing to eschew economic profits but anchored by personal reserves of capital in its various forms creating a “distance from necessity” that instils them with an outward appearance of ease (Bourdieu 2010, 48).

## Background and Theory
The international prestige of the organizing publishers has a multiplying effect on the Novel Prize’s built-in symbolic capital. Fourteen authors published by New Directions have won the Nobel Prize, while four have been published by Fitzcarraldo; Giramondo published 2023 laureate Jon Fosse’s _Septology_ in Australia a year prior to Fosse’s win. Associations with the Nobel Prize heighten the cultural legitimacy of the presses. Particularly in the case of Fitzcarraldo, Nobel Prize successes afforded the press valuable media visibility while it was still relatively young. With their imprints suggestive of literary quality, being published by these prestigious presses is itself a form of consecration. This, it seems, is a primary appeal of entering the Novel Prize. In a 2022 interview with Melissa Cranenburgh on Melbourne radio station _3RRR_, Au identified the attraction of entering her manuscript to the prize as the access it provided to the three prestigious publishers, rather than winning the prize itself. Asked why she entered the prize, Au responded that “I just really admired all three publishers” and hoped that one might acquire her novella through the process (Cranenburgh [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR15 "Cranenburgh, Melissa. 2022. “Jessica Au.” Interview of Jessica Au. Backstory. 3RRR. February 2.   
                  https://www.rrr.org.au/explore/podcasts/backstory/episodes/5689-jessica-au

## Background and Theory
."), 33, 50). In press releases following the announcement of Au as the inaugural winner, the author’s comments were repeatedly in gratitude for being able to work with the three publishers, of whom she is a “huge admirer” (Cowdrey [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR14 "Cowdrey, Katherine. 2021. “Jessica Au Named Inaugural Winner of The Novel Prize.” The Bookseller, February 10.   
                  https://www.thebookseller.com/rights/jessica-au-named-inaugural-winner-novel-prize-1236876  
                    
                .")), and it had been “a dream and a privilege to get the chance to work with them” (Giramondo [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR24 "Giramondo Publishing. 2022. “‘Can we truly know another’s inner world?’—Jessica Au on Cold Enough for Snow.” Giramondo Publishing, December 5.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/jessica-au-cold-enough-for-snow-laguna  
                    
                .")). For Au, then, associating with these publishers carried an inherent prestige. Similar statements of admiration of the organizing publishers recur in statements from subsequent winners of the prize: Anne de Marken credited the publishers with “integrity and imaginative force” (Giramondo [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR25 "Giramondo Publishing. 2023. “Anne de Marcken and Jonathan Buckley Are Joint Winners of the 2022 Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, March 22.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/anne-de-marcken-and-jonathan-buckley-are-joint-winners-of-the-2022-novel-prize/  
                    

## Background and Theory
                .")); Jonathan Buckley called them “three of the boldest and most exciting publishers of contemporary writing” (Giramondo [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR25 "Giramondo Publishing. 2023. “Anne de Marcken and Jonathan Buckley Are Joint Winners of the 2022 Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, March 22.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/anne-de-marcken-and-jonathan-buckley-are-joint-winners-of-the-2022-novel-prize/  
                    
                .")). The authors are reflecting their symbolic capital gains from winning the prize back onto the awarding publishers, whose recognized prestige is the source of this capital. Unlike other literary awards, the symbolic value of the Novel Prize is entangled with the perceptions of the value of the publishers themselves, rather than being bestowed by state, commercial, or independent bodies.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
The Novel Prize operates as both an acquisition strategy for the three literary publishers and as a literary award. In some ways, the Novel Prize diminishes perceptions of the former in favor of being received as the latter. For example, descriptions of the Novel Prize are often obscure in the presentation of the prize money being an advance against royalties. The announcements of each of the three winners and the press releases advertising entry into the prize describe how “it offers US$10,000 to the winner and simultaneous publication” (Giramondo [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR25 "Giramondo Publishing. 2023. “Anne de Marcken and Jonathan Buckley Are Joint Winners of the 2022 Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, March 22.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/anne-de-marcken-and-jonathan-buckley-are-joint-winners-of-the-2022-novel-prize/
.")); only in the original press release announcing the prize and in the closing paragraphs of the 2020 and 2022 shortlist announcements is it clarified that this prize money is “in the form of an advance against royalties” (Giramondo [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR22 "Giramondo Publishing. 2020. “Giramondo Publishing, Fitzcarraldo Editions and New Directions launch The Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, February 28.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/giramondo-publishing-fitzcarraldo-editions-and-new-directions-launch-the-novel-prize  
                    
                .")). Although this seems like a minor alteration, diminishing the status of the award as being one for an unpublished manuscript and so giving the competition the appearance of being a post-publication literary award heightens the perceived legitimacy of prize by obscuring economic considerations.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
The Novel Prize is a reordered approach to slush piles, a formerly physical but now likely digital stack of unsolicited queries and manuscripts from authors and agents seeking publication. Giramondo are the only Novel Prize publisher who accept unsolicited manuscripts, albeit during a limited window each year. While unsolicited manuscripts may enable presses to unearth obscure literary works, they can be labor intensive for small publishers. New Directions stress this on their website, noting that their decision to not accept unsolicited manuscripts is due to the house being “understaffed” and needing to preserve their time and money to continue publishing (New Directions n.d. b). Fitzcarraldo also do not accept unsolicited submissions, but through the Novel Prize, the new Poetry in Translation Prize, and their solo-run Fitzcarraldo Editions/Mahler & LeWitt Studios Essay Prize, the house can still solicit new work across fiction, poetry, and non-fiction respectively. The Novel Prize functions as a slush pile for the organizing publishers, albeit with greater control and presented with more prestige.
While most major prizes draw their juries from a mix of novelists, critics, academics, agents, and celebrities, the Novel Prize is judged exclusively by editors. This is a highly consequential choice. As James English ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR17 "English, James F. 2005. The Economy of Prestige: Prizes, Awards, and the Circulation of Cultural Value. Harvard University Press.   
                  https://doi.org/10.4159/9780674036536

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
.")) argues, the prestige of a literary prize is inseparable from the symbolic capital of those who judge it. Jurors bring with them accumulated cultural, social, and professional authority that is transferred to the prize itself. The composition of a judging panel is thus a useful way to understand how a prize is positioned by its organizers. The 2025 Miles Franklin Literary Award was judged by four literary scholars and chaired by a senior librarian at the State Library of New South Wales, which positioned the prize as more immediately concerned with literary quality, with the judges’ authority here predicated on their cultural capital. The 2025 Booker Prize judging panel, on the other hand, demonstrated a greater concern with broad appeal, featuring Kiley Reid, a _New York Times_ bestselling author, Chris Powers, former host of BBC Radio 4’s _Open Book_ show, and Sarah Jessica Parker, a celebrity actor. The trophy was awarded to winning author David Szaly by Queen Camilla of the United Kingdom, further heightening the potential media interest in the prize ceremony. The Booker’s use of celebrities to encourage media attention is striking given that, in her 2014 study, Driscoll noted the significant choice of the Booker Prize organizers until that point _not_ including a celebrity on the judging panel, as other awards tended to do.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
By making editors its exclusive judges, the Novel Prize symbolically repositions editorial labour as a primary source of literary legitimacy in a publishing economy otherwise dominated by agents, marketing departments, and algorithmic visibility. In a 2015 article for the _Sydney Review of Books,_ Giramondo’s Indyk attacked how literary prizes favored “appeal” over literary innovation, and derided having to spend “thousands of dollars in entry fees” every year: other than abolishing literary prizes, Indyk suggested that the judgement of literary quality should be given to those “who have a critical training in literature, a good knowledge of literary history, and a wide acquaintance with contemporary writing in all its genres”(Indyk[2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR33 "Indyk, Ivor. 2015. “The Cult of the Middlebrow.” Sydney Review of Books, September 4.   
                  https://sydneyreviewofbooks.com/essays/the-cult-of-the-middlebrow
.")). The Novel Prize seems to fulfil Indyk’s ideal for the judging composition of literary prizes. The conglomeration of the publishing industry had progressively weakened the editor’s role in the production of literary value: where editors once functioned as cultural gatekeepers who discovered and shaped new writers, that role had increasingly been displaced by literary agents, who now occupy a dominant position in identifying and circulating new fiction within bureaucratised publishing houses (Sinykin 2023). Lacking the economic capital of multinational firms, these independents have sought to re-center the editor as a figure of cultural authority and aesthetic judgment. The Novel Prize attempts to restore the editor not merely as a professional intermediary but as a public consecrator of literary value.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
There are a host of other awards for unpublished manuscripts in Australia. These range from those run by other independent presses as acquisition strategies, such as Fremantle Press’s Fogerty Literary Award; those run by larger houses, such as the Vogel Literary Award, which ceased in 2024, guaranteeing publication with Allen & Unwin; or the Victorian Premier’s Unpublished Manuscript Award, facilitated by the Victorian state government, which does not offer publication, although the symbolic capital has helped winners subsequently acquire publishing deals. Each of these prizes seek to instill an as-yet-unpublished novel with the symbolic capital that comes from winning an award in the hope of increasing the short-term sales of the book upon launch: acquiring a book through the competition which then enters the market already bearing a stamp of legitimacy. However, while these awards have helped to launch successful international careers—for example, Tim Winton’s debut novel _An Open Swimmer_ (1982) won the Vogel Literary Award in 1981—none of these awards have the built-in international connections of the Novel Prize and the guarantee of international editions. This is likewise true of other manuscript prizes in the international anglophone field. The transnationality of the Novel Prize compared to other manuscript prizes is largely facilitated by this prize’s inauguration in a post-digital reading world: the practicality of running such a prize is underpinned by digital communications, while reading communities can be more geographically dispersed through the affordances of social media.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
There is a further sense that the Novel Prize, at least for Giramondo, is attempting to correct perceived deficiencies in the extent to which the publisher was benefitting from the traditional literary awards. Within the Australian field of literary prizes, in particular, it seems that prizes have not been as successful in converting symbolic capital into economic capital as one might expect. Emmett Stinson has suggested that, as of 2016, “only a handful of Australian prizes reliably boost sales,” most notably from the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the Stella Prize (2019, 214). Indyk’s Boisbouvier Oration at the 2019 Melbourne Writers Festival considered the different mechanisms of valuing Australian literature. This annual speech at the Melbourne Writers Festival is an extension of the University of Melbourne’s Boisbouvier Chair in Australian Literature, founded in 2015 to inspire public engagement with Australian literature, with the speeches often reflecting on the role and value of Australian literature. Prizes, Indyk suggested, do not guarantee sales on their own: although the prize money will benefit a literary author, Indyk noted that Brian Castro’s _Blindness and Rage: A Phantasmagoria_ (2017) winning the Prime Minister’s Literary Award in 2018 only equated to roughly fifty sales of the book in the following six months. He compared this to the _New York Times Magazine_ stating in 2018 that another Giramondo author, Gerald Murnane, was “the greatest living English-language writer most people have never heard of,” which had more of an impact on sales: “because the _New York Times_ said it, people sat up, and took notice” (Indyk [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR34 "Indyk, Ivor. 2020. “Publishing from the Provinces.” Sydney Review of Books, February 17.   
                  https://sydneyreviewofbooks.com/essays/publishing-from-the-provinces
.")).

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
The consecration of Australian literature, in other words, is expedited by prestigious intermediaries from the anglophone centers: in this instance, a review from a New York publication meant more to sales than a prize in Australia. This is in line with Pascale Casanova’s (2004) world literary system, wherein appearing to participate in a transcendent literary ‘present’ beyond national borders and mediated by international literary centers was a key means to accrue symbolic capital. As a literary prize that awards a universal aesthetic beyond national borders, the Nobel Prize had become for Casanova “the highest honour the world republic of letters has to give” (2004, 94). This idea of borderless literary community is likewise encapsulated in the Novel Prize. The more peripherally located Giramondo would theoretically be the greatest beneficiary of this arrangement with their New York and London counterparts, with a book such as Au’s receiving built-in approval from the dominant anglophone markets from its simultaneous publication, and with a clear path to further consecration through reviews in periodicals in those countries.

## Au’s International Reception
After winning publication through the Novel Prize, _Cold Enough for Snow_ was quickly elevated through the traditional auspices of literary consecration. Au has stated that winning the prize “opened up opportunities that the book would never have had” (Giramondo [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR24 "Giramondo Publishing. 2022. “‘Can we truly know another’s inner world?’—Jessica Au on Cold Enough for Snow.” Giramondo Publishing, December 5.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/jessica-au-cold-enough-for-snow-laguna
.")). While presenting itself as a particularly literary prize and lacking the glamourous award ceremony or media visibility of more mainstream prizes, this winner of the Novel Prize benefitted in similar ways.
_Cold Enough for Snow_ has been translated into an impressive eighteen languages since its release (AustLit n.d.). World rights are jointly controlled by the three publishers, which maximized the potential for international sales. Indeed, there was strong international interest in the novella prior to its publication, with rights to Catalan, French, German, Italian, Romanian, Spanish, and Turkish publishers already sold in March 2021 (Books+Publishing [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR23 "Giramondo Publishing. 2021. “Cold Enough for Snow by Jessica Au wins The Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, February 11.   
                  https://giramondopublishing.com/jessica-au-wins-the-novel-prize

## Au’s International Reception
.")). _Cold Enough for Snow_ has received at least twelve reviews in literary journals and magazines outside Australia since its publication. This includes reviews in influential New York City periodicals _The New York Times_ and _The New Yorker_. It has been excerpted in the prestigious London literary magazine _Granta_ (Au [2022b](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR3 "Au, Jessica. 2022b. “Cold Enough for Snow.” Granta, February 8.   
                  https://granta.com/cold-enough-for-snow  
                    
                .")) and the author interviewed in New York City’s _BOMB Magazine_ (Lucas [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR39 "Lucas, Madeline. 2022. “Chasing the Echoes of Belonging: Jessica Au Interviewed.” BOMB Magazine, April 13.   
                  https://bombmagazine.org/articles/2022/04/13/jessica-au-interviewed  
                    
                .")). The novella subsequently won a plethora of Australia’s national literary prizes: the 2022 Readings Prize for Fiction; the 2023 Prime Minister’s Literary Award for Fiction; the Victorian Premier’s Prize for Fiction and the Victorian Prize for Literature in 2023. Au’s novella has already begun to see consideration from literary academics, with an academic article by Gretchen Shirm ([2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR46 "Shirm, Gretchen. 2025. “The Myth of ‘Wound’ Writing: The Multiple Surfaces of Jessica Au’s Cold Enough for Snow.” Life Writing 22 (1): 105–21.   
                  https://doi.org/10.1080/14484528.2023.2257903  
                    

## Au’s International Reception
                .")) published in Q1 journal _Life Writing_ (SCImago n.d.). This is another important step for a literary novel’s symbolic capital to be converted into economic capital, as inclusion on academic reading lists promotes ongoing backlist sales.
In lieu of sales figures, the volume of ratings on the platform Goodreads compared to other Giramondo novels is a striking testament to the large readership that the Novel Prize’s inaugural winner found. _Cold Enough for Snow_ had 19,900 reader ratings on Goodreads as of February 2026, including 3,000 reviews, a very wide readership for a novel published by Giramondo. Alexis Wright’s _Praiseworthy_ (2023), which won major national literary awards in Australia and was also published by New Directions in the US market and by literary press And Other Stories in the UK market, had 809 ratings at the same time. _Praiseworthy_ is a less accessible book than Au’s novella, being long and dealing with Aboriginal themes which may not appeal to a global audience. Yet Gerald Murnane’s _Border Districts_ (2017) is of a similar length to _Cold Enough for Snow_, which also won the Prime Minister’s Literary Award for Fiction in 2018, and has been published by literary press Farrar, Straus and Giroux in the US market and by And Other Stories in the UK market. _Border Districts_ had received 1,090 ratings on Goodreads, also a fraction of the attention of _Cold Enough for Snow._ The volume of Goodreads ratings is not an entirely stable way of comparing readerships, especially given that we suspect that readers of Wright and Murnane are less likely to use Goodreads as a platform. Yet the difference in ratings suggests the broader appeal that Au’s novella found following its Novel Prize win than is usual for a Giramondo book. This may also suggest that judging for the Novel Prize was more concerned with the mainstream appeal of its inaugural winner than the prize description suggests.

## Au’s International Reception
To demonstrate how reception of _Cold Enough for Snow_ seems to be an extension of the presentation of the Novel Prize, we collected and analyzed twelve international reviews of Au’s novella from literary journals, magazines, and news outlets. These were manually sourced through searches of the novella’s title on Google Search and X. Published between 2021 to 2024, these reviews are themselves a testament to the prolonged critical attention afforded to this Novel Prize winner. For comparison, _Praiseworthy_ only received reviews from two of the same outlets as Au’s novellaFootnote 1; _Border Districts_ received more attention, being reviewed by five of the same outlets,Footnote 2 and was further reviewed in other symbolically rich outlets such as the _London Review of Books_ and _The Washington Post_, although Murnane was enjoying an international renaissance during this period, led by New York literary journalists (Stinson [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR50 "Stinson, Emmett. 2025. “Gerald Murnane’s Transnational Reception.” Mémoires Du Livre / Studies in Book Culture 16 (2): 1–24.   
                  https://doi.org/10.7202/1122229ar
.")). Analyzing the common themes of these reviews through close reading illuminates how Au’s reception by international and symbolically rich readers reproduced the strategic fashioning of the Novel Prize.

## Au’s International Reception
Our use of reviews to gauge the reception of _Cold Enough for Snow_ is informed by Melinda Harvey and Julieanne Lamond’s (2019) study of review coverage of Australian prize winners, which found that prize-winning books are the most reviewed by Australian outlets. Albeit focused on the national rather than international space, this study is a useful touchstone. Prizes and reviews have a relationship of “interdependence and amplification,” whereby success in one usually guarantees success in the other, given that both institutions share systems of value, and, usually, personnel (Harvey and Lamond 2019, 231). An intriguing thread in this essay is Harvey and Lamond’s consideration of prizes for unpublished manuscripts, which have altered the usual consecratory timeline of a novel’s life cycle by “undermining” the consecratory priority of book reviewers (2019, 236): they found that recipients of unpublished manuscript prizes were likely to receive major reviews and further awards upon their publication, with reviewers drawn to texts already imbued with symbolic value.
Two common features across these reviews reinforce the strategic self-fashioning of the Novel Prize: these reviews demonstrate the perceived literary quality of _Cold Enough for Snow_, as well as the perceived internationalism of the Novel Prize, with the novella being treated as an international rather than Australian text.

## Au’s International Reception
### Perceptions of Excellence
The twelve international reviews are generally positive, perhaps due to an expected level of literary achievement in _Cold Enough for Snow_, given its prize-winning status and association with the three prestigious publishers. Reviewers contrast Au’s depictions of the narrator’s interiority with the sparsity of the novella’s plot. This positions the book as literary in its denial of the plot and character derived pleasures of popular fiction; these differentiating criteria in the reception of the perceived popular and high art have been extensively studied in reference to film reviews (Baumann [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR6 "Baumann, Shyon. 2001. “Intellectualization and Art World Development: Film in the United States.” American Sociological Review 66 (3): 404–426.   
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/000312240106600305

The Booker describes itself as awarding a book “that not only speaks to our current times, but also one that will endure and join the pantheon of great literature” (The Booker Prize n.d.), foregrounding thematic urgency and potential canonicity.
The Novel Prize reframes the site of value from appeal and thematic urgency to formal and aesthetic practice, presenting itself as a prize for the novel as a literary form. The Novel Prize thus reinforces the literary position-taking of the organizing publishers within the largely conglomerated publishing space, through which it derives its power to consecrate texts without external legitimation. Dan Sinykin’s _Big Fiction_ (2023) has studied this shift to conglomeration in the American market, which he identifies as intensifying in the 1980s and producing a recalibration of the whole literary field. Sinykin notes how conglomeration incentivized smaller presses, in this case New Directions, to “claim authenticity by differentiating oneself from a sell-out” (2023, 127). In other words, amplifying their pursuit of cultural over economic value had become a branding opportunity for smaller presses to differentiate themselves and assert their value to the field. The “About” pages on the websites of Giramondo and Fitzcarraldo both describe the respective presses as publishing “innovative” books with an international tilt (Giramondo n.d. b; Fitzcarraldo n.d.). The New Directions “About Us” page is brief, a short anecdote of founder James Laughlin being urged by modernist poet Ezra Pound to “do something useful” after graduating from Harvard University (New Directions n.d. a). Nevertheless, even this anecdote aligns New Directions with innovative aesthetics and global literary community through the invocation of Pound, while publicly demonstrating the social and cultural capital of the founder.

The shared approach to publishing books of perceived cultural value over those of immediate economic value is largely underpinned by secure financial foundations. ## Background and Theory
The international prestige of the organizing publishers has a multiplying effect on the Novel Prize’s built-in symbolic capital. Fourteen authors published by New Directions have won the Nobel Prize, while four have been published by Fitzcarraldo; Giramondo published 2023 laureate Jon Fosse’s _Septology_ in Australia a year prior to Fosse’s win. The Novel Prize operates as both an acquisition strategy for the three literary publishers and as a literary award. In some ways, the Novel Prize diminishes perceptions of the former in favor of being received as the latter. For example, descriptions of the Novel Prize are often obscure in the presentation of the prize money being an advance against royalties. The announcements of each of the three winners and the press releases advertising entry into the prize describe how “it offers US$10,000 to the winner and simultaneous publication” (Giramondo [2023](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR25 "Giramondo Publishing. 2023. “Anne de Marcken and Jonathan Buckley Are Joint Winners of the 2022 Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, March 22.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
The Novel Prize is a reordered approach to slush piles, a formerly physical but now likely digital stack of unsolicited queries and manuscripts from authors and agents seeking publication. Giramondo are the only Novel Prize publisher who accept unsolicited manuscripts, albeit during a limited window each year. While unsolicited manuscripts may enable presses to unearth obscure literary works, they can be labor intensive for small publishers. New Directions stress this on their website, noting that their decision to not accept unsolicited manuscripts is due to the house being “understaffed” and needing to preserve their time and money to continue publishing (New Directions n.d. b). Fitzcarraldo also do not accept unsolicited submissions, but through the Novel Prize, the new Poetry in Translation Prize, and their solo-run Fitzcarraldo Editions/Mahler & LeWitt Studios Essay Prize, the house can still solicit new work across fiction, poetry, and non-fiction respectively. The Novel Prize functions as a slush pile for the organizing publishers, albeit with greater control and presented with more prestige.
While most major prizes draw their juries from a mix of novelists, critics, academics, agents, and celebrities, the Novel Prize is judged exclusively by editors. This is a highly consequential choice. As James English ([2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR17 "English, James F. 2005. The Economy of Prestige: Prizes, Awards, and the Circulation of Cultural Value. Harvard University Press.   
                  https://doi.org/10.4159/9780674036536

Jurors bring with them accumulated cultural, social, and professional authority that is transferred to the prize itself. The composition of a judging panel is thus a useful way to understand how a prize is positioned by its organizers. The 2025 Miles Franklin Literary Award was judged by four literary scholars and chaired by a senior librarian at the State Library of New South Wales, which positioned the prize as more immediately concerned with literary quality, with the judges’ authority here predicated on their cultural capital. The 2025 Booker Prize judging panel, on the other hand, demonstrated a greater concern with broad appeal, featuring Kiley Reid, a _New York Times_ bestselling author, Chris Powers, former host of BBC Radio 4’s _Open Book_ show, and Sarah Jessica Parker, a celebrity actor. The trophy was awarded to winning author David Szaly by Queen Camilla of the United Kingdom, further heightening the potential media interest in the prize ceremony. The Booker’s use of celebrities to encourage media attention is striking given that, in her 2014 study, Driscoll noted the significant choice of the Booker Prize organizers until that point _not_ including a celebrity on the judging panel, as other awards tended to do.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
By making editors its exclusive judges, the Novel Prize symbolically repositions editorial labour as a primary source of literary legitimacy in a publishing economy otherwise dominated by agents, marketing departments, and algorithmic visibility. In a 2015 article for the _Sydney Review of Books,_ Giramondo’s Indyk attacked how literary prizes favored “appeal” over literary innovation, and derided having to spend “thousands of dollars in entry fees” every year: other than abolishing literary prizes, Indyk suggested that the judgement of literary quality should be given to those “who have a critical training in literature, a good knowledge of literary history, and a wide acquaintance with contemporary writing in all its genres”(Indyk[2015](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR33 "Indyk, Ivor. 2015. “The Cult of the Middlebrow.” Sydney Review of Books, September 4.   
                  https://sydneyreviewofbooks.com/essays/the-cult-of-the-middlebrow
.")). The Novel Prize seems to fulfil Indyk’s ideal for the judging composition of literary prizes. The conglomeration of the publishing industry had progressively weakened the editor’s role in the production of literary value: where editors once functioned as cultural gatekeepers who discovered and shaped new writers, that role had increasingly been displaced by literary agents, who now occupy a dominant position in identifying and circulating new fiction within bureaucratised publishing houses (Sinykin 2023). Lacking the economic capital of multinational firms, these independents have sought to re-center the editor as a figure of cultural authority and aesthetic judgment. The Novel Prize attempts to restore the editor not merely as a professional intermediary but as a public consecrator of literary value.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
There are a host of other awards for unpublished manuscripts in Australia. These range from those run by other independent presses as acquisition strategies, such as Fremantle Press’s Fogerty Literary Award; those run by larger houses, such as the Vogel Literary Award, which ceased in 2024, guaranteeing publication with Allen & Unwin; or the Victorian Premier’s Unpublished Manuscript Award, facilitated by the Victorian state government, which does not offer publication, although the symbolic capital has helped winners subsequently acquire publishing deals. Each of these prizes seek to instill an as-yet-unpublished novel with the symbolic capital that comes from winning an award in the hope of increasing the short-term sales of the book upon launch: acquiring a book through the competition which then enters the market already bearing a stamp of legitimacy. However, while these awards have helped to launch successful international careers—for example, Tim Winton’s debut novel _An Open Swimmer_ (1982) won the Vogel Literary Award in 1981—none of these awards have the built-in international connections of the Novel Prize and the guarantee of international editions. This is likewise true of other manuscript prizes in the international anglophone field. The transnationality of the Novel Prize compared to other manuscript prizes is largely facilitated by this prize’s inauguration in a post-digital reading world: the practicality of running such a prize is underpinned by digital communications, while reading communities can be more geographically dispersed through the affordances of social media.

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
There is a further sense that the Novel Prize, at least for Giramondo, is attempting to correct perceived deficiencies in the extent to which the publisher was benefitting from the traditional literary awards. Within the Australian field of literary prizes, in particular, it seems that prizes have not been as successful in converting symbolic capital into economic capital as one might expect. Emmett Stinson has suggested that, as of 2016, “only a handful of Australian prizes reliably boost sales,” most notably from the Miles Franklin Literary Award and the Stella Prize (2019, 214). Indyk’s Boisbouvier Oration at the 2019 Melbourne Writers Festival considered the different mechanisms of valuing Australian literature. This annual speech at the Melbourne Writers Festival is an extension of the University of Melbourne’s Boisbouvier Chair in Australian Literature, founded in 2015 to inspire public engagement with Australian literature, with the speeches often reflecting on the role and value of Australian literature. Prizes, Indyk suggested, do not guarantee sales on their own: although the prize money will benefit a literary author, Indyk noted that Brian Castro’s _Blindness and Rage: A Phantasmagoria_ (2017) winning the Prime Minister’s Literary Award in 2018 only equated to roughly fifty sales of the book in the following six months. He compared this to the _New York Times Magazine_ stating in 2018 that another Giramondo author, Gerald Murnane, was “the greatest living English-language writer most people have never heard of,” which had more of an impact on sales: “because the _New York Times_ said it, people sat up, and took notice” (Indyk [2020](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR34 "Indyk, Ivor. 2020. “Publishing from the Provinces.” Sydney Review of Books, February 17.   
                  https://sydneyreviewofbooks.com/essays/publishing-from-the-provinces
.")).

## Background and Theory
### Prizing an Unpublished Manuscript
The consecration of Australian literature, in other words, is expedited by prestigious intermediaries from the anglophone centers: in this instance, a review from a New York publication meant more to sales than a prize in Australia. This is in line with Pascale Casanova’s (2004) world literary system, wherein appearing to participate in a transcendent literary ‘present’ beyond national borders and mediated by international literary centers was a key means to accrue symbolic capital. As a literary prize that awards a universal aesthetic beyond national borders, the Nobel Prize had become for Casanova “the highest honour the world republic of letters has to give” (2004, 94). This idea of borderless literary community is likewise encapsulated in the Novel Prize. The more peripherally located Giramondo would theoretically be the greatest beneficiary of this arrangement with their New York and London counterparts, with a book such as Au’s receiving built-in approval from the dominant anglophone markets from its simultaneous publication, and with a clear path to further consecration through reviews in periodicals in those countries.

## Au’s International Reception
After winning publication through the Novel Prize, _Cold Enough for Snow_ was quickly elevated through the traditional auspices of literary consecration. Au has stated that winning the prize “opened up opportunities that the book would never have had” (Giramondo [2022](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR24 "Giramondo Publishing. 2022. “‘Can we truly know another’s inner world?’—Jessica Au on Cold Enough for Snow.” Giramondo Publishing, December 5.

.")). While presenting itself as a particularly literary prize and lacking the glamourous award ceremony or media visibility of more mainstream prizes, this winner of the Novel Prize benefitted in similar ways.
_Cold Enough for Snow_ has been translated into an impressive eighteen languages since its release (AustLit n.d.). World rights are jointly controlled by the three publishers, which maximized the potential for international sales. Indeed, there was strong international interest in the novella prior to its publication, with rights to Catalan, French, German, Italian, Romanian, Spanish, and Turkish publishers already sold in March 2021 (Books+Publishing [2021](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR23 "Giramondo Publishing. 2021. “Cold Enough for Snow by Jessica Au wins The Novel Prize.” Giramondo Publishing, February 11.

In lieu of sales figures, the volume of ratings on the platform Goodreads compared to other Giramondo novels is a striking testament to the large readership that the Novel Prize’s inaugural winner found. _Cold Enough for Snow_ had 19,900 reader ratings on Goodreads as of February 2026, including 3,000 reviews, a very wide readership for a novel published by Giramondo. Alexis Wright’s _Praiseworthy_ (2023), which won major national literary awards in Australia and was also published by New Directions in the US market and by literary press And Other Stories in the UK market, had 809 ratings at the same time. _Praiseworthy_ is a less accessible book than Au’s novella, being long and dealing with Aboriginal themes which may not appeal to a global audience. Yet Gerald Murnane’s _Border Districts_ (2017) is of a similar length to _Cold Enough for Snow_, which also won the Prime Minister’s Literary Award for Fiction in 2018, and has been published by literary press Farrar, Straus and Giroux in the US market and by And Other Stories in the UK market. _Border Districts_ had received 1,090 ratings on Goodreads, also a fraction of the attention of _Cold Enough for Snow._ The volume of Goodreads ratings is not an entirely stable way of comparing readerships, especially given that we suspect that readers of Wright and Murnane are less likely to use Goodreads as a platform. Yet the difference in ratings suggests the broader appeal that Au’s novella found following its Novel Prize win than is usual for a Giramondo book. This may also suggest that judging for the Novel Prize was more concerned with the mainstream appeal of its inaugural winner than the prize description suggests.

## Au’s International Reception
To demonstrate how reception of _Cold Enough for Snow_ seems to be an extension of the presentation of the Novel Prize, we collected and analyzed twelve international reviews of Au’s novella from literary journals, magazines, and news outlets. These were manually sourced through searches of the novella’s title on Google Search and X. Published between 2021 to 2024, these reviews are themselves a testament to the prolonged critical attention afforded to this Novel Prize winner. For comparison, _Praiseworthy_ only received reviews from two of the same outlets as Au’s novellaFootnote 1; _Border Districts_ received more attention, being reviewed by five of the same outlets,Footnote 2 and was further reviewed in other symbolically rich outlets such as the _London Review of Books_ and _The Washington Post_, although Murnane was enjoying an international renaissance during this period, led by New York literary journalists (Stinson [2025](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR50 "Stinson, Emmett. 2025. “Gerald Murnane’s Transnational Reception.” Mémoires Du Livre / Studies in Book Culture 16 (2): 1–24.   
                  https://doi.org/10.7202/1122229ar
.")). Analyzing the common themes of these reviews through close reading illuminates how Au’s reception by international and symbolically rich readers reproduced the strategic fashioning of the Novel Prize.

## Au’s International Reception
Our use of reviews to gauge the reception of _Cold Enough for Snow_ is informed by Melinda Harvey and Julieanne Lamond’s (2019) study of review coverage of Australian prize winners, which found that prize-winning books are the most reviewed by Australian outlets. Albeit focused on the national rather than international space, this study is a useful touchstone. Prizes and reviews have a relationship of “interdependence and amplification,” whereby success in one usually guarantees success in the other, given that both institutions share systems of value, and, usually, personnel (Harvey and Lamond 2019, 231). An intriguing thread in this essay is Harvey and Lamond’s consideration of prizes for unpublished manuscripts, which have altered the usual consecratory timeline of a novel’s life cycle by “undermining” the consecratory priority of book reviewers (2019, 236): they found that recipients of unpublished manuscript prizes were likely to receive major reviews and further awards upon their publication, with reviewers drawn to texts already imbued with symbolic value.
Two common features across these reviews reinforce the strategic self-fashioning of the Novel Prize: these reviews demonstrate the perceived literary quality of _Cold Enough for Snow_, as well as the perceived internationalism of the Novel Prize, with the novella being treated as an international rather than Australian text.

## Au’s International Reception
### Perceptions of Excellence
The twelve international reviews are generally positive, perhaps due to an expected level of literary achievement in _Cold Enough for Snow_, given its prize-winning status and association with the three prestigious publishers. Reviewers contrast Au’s depictions of the narrator’s interiority with the sparsity of the novella’s plot. This positions the book as literary in its denial of the plot and character derived pleasures of popular fiction; these differentiating criteria in the reception of the perceived popular and high art have been extensively studied in reference to film reviews (Baumann [2001](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s12109-026-10089-1#ref-CR6 "Baumann, Shyon. 2001. “Intellectualization and Art World Development: Film in the United States.” American Sociological Review 66 (3): 404–426.   
                  https://doi.org/10.1177/000312240106600305

Title: Interview with Kelly J. Ford, Author of The Hunt
Chunks: 0,1,2,3,4,5,6,7
In the Arkansas of Kelly J. Ford’s third novel, _The Hunt_, Easter season does not mean pink bows and bunnies. It means bored or needy townspeople seeking a golden egg and prize money. Gossips and greedy sponsors seeking social currency and sales. Zealous Christians seeking recruits and redemption. Most of all, it means a disappearance and, usually, a death. Is there a seasonal serial killer on the loose? Will this year produce another victim?
Called “a modern master of the rural noir” and celebrated by Best Thriller Books for her “ability to draw readers into the chaos and craziness of everyday life while exploring themes of shared trauma, family dynamics, and the societal constraints of small-town America,” Kelly J. Ford has written her most multi-dimensional novel yet, introducing us to a compelling cast of characters whose humanity matters as much as their survival. What a treat to Zoom with her and learn about her fascinations, frustrations, and factory jobs on the way to her latest success.
**_The Hunt_****is populated with seekers, and you turn your readers into seekers, too. We _must_ figure out what’s going on in Presley. How much were you a seeker as you wrote the story? Did you know where it was headed?**
Whenever I’m writing, I’m always seeking because I never know the end. I feel like every draft, I’m just seeking the story. I have been using a lot of power tools lately that are breaking, and I have to take them apart. I’m like, “Well, you don’t know how to fix it until you take it apart.” So I try to apply that to revision. I’ll start a draft, and then I’ll go back through, and I’ll read it. And I’m like, “You know, this isn’t working. I need to fix this.” And so I kind of tear apart my drafts as I go. I might find something more interesting in a later draft and change my idea of what the ending is. The endings are so hard to land. You want something that’s resonant.
**Did you know if there was going to _be_ a hunter?**

I didn’t. I’m one of those readers who likes things a little bit ambiguous. I’m very much like a townsperson in the hunt: What _is_ going on? Who _is_ behind all of this? I start with this cast of characters, and I know how each of them ticks. For every single character, it’s like, What do they want? What is their obstacle? What are they going to do to get it? Once you have those kind of built-in engines, you can just let your plot go. And then it’s kind of fun. You go into that wonderful, trance-like state, and you start to figure it out, and then it’s almost like, “Oh, my God! _That’s_ what happened!”
**How did you determine the size of your character cast? Since everybody you introduce is a potential suspect or victim, I wondered if you felt your cast would get out of hand or if you felt, “No, it has to be this big.”**
This book is kind of the culmination of two other books that I trunked. I already had some characters that I really loved. I took two main characters that already existed from those books and put them into this book. And somehow, it worked. I knew I wanted Nell, and I knew I wanted Elijah, and they seemed like a perfect fit together: aunt and nephew bound by this circumstance of Elijah’s father going missing, and then his subsequent death, which many in town attribute to a serial killer. And when there’s a serial killer, you kind of don’t have a choice but to have a lot of characters. Inevitably, you have a giant cast.

But I also really love Jami Attenberg’s _The Middlesteins_. I love that book, and I was always like, “I would love to have a book that has all these characters and be able to see if I can do it.” The world of _Cottonmouths_, my debut, was so small—very few characters, very claustrophobic—and so it felt like a pressure cooker. And then _Real Bad Things_ was, again, not a ton of characters. So in a way, I just wanted to have fun and expand my cast. Then by nature of choosing Elijah… well, Elijah is 17 years old, so that [determined] a lot of the plotting. And not even plotting. More like logistics. Between me and my editor and my copy editor and the proofreader, we’re all like, “Wait a minute, what year is it?” We had all these lists written down, like, this is the year that this person died, and how they died…
**Why was Elijah so pivotal? It sounds as though you built your whole timeframe around him.**
Yeah, I just wanted to focus on the individuals impacted by these deaths. You know, thinking about things like true crime—the spectacle of true crime, but also the fascination with it—I mean, I’ll read a lot of that, but there is something icky about it at times. There are real people behind it. Elijah is pivotal in that it’s his father, it’s a loss, he never knew him, and there’s this entire event in town where everyone’s in a frenzy. And his father is the rumored first victim. That to me is so compelling, putting yourself into a person’s shoes. Our characters are people. They’re not just characters; they’re individuals that we live with for a long time. What must it be like for someone who has this hole in their heart? What must that feel like, especially when you never got to know them as a person and you can’t truly move on? Because there’s not real closure. I’m always fascinated by that angle of a crime. I’m just always fascinated with psychology. There are a lot of really excellent books that go into victim stories. So I wanted to bring that into it.
**For the most part, the novel tracks Nell and Ada using close third-person narration. Why did you decide to center both women’s experiences?**

They present two sides of the town. One side is like, “This hunt should not happen, even if there’s not a serial killer. There are deaths associated with it every year.” And this side is convinced it’s because of the hunt, serial killer or not. Nell, whose brother was affected, is more toward this side. But then on the other side, you’ve got people like Ada, who is an avid Egghead, someone who loves the hunt, who is more logical, thinking, “Of course people are going to get hurt. Nobody’s doing anything, and then suddenly everyone goes out and is active in the community, looking around, not paying attention, so you know, of course accidents happen.” I just wanted to have that closeness for both sides. I also wanted to present a different perspective on these working-class women in Arkansas. You don’t see that all the time, especially in Southern fiction, where the working class is often typical cisgender white males; they’re the ones working at the factories and having a hard time. So then it’s like, _I’ve_ worked in a factory, two factories in college.
**What did you do?**
Oh, my gosh. So the first one, you know microwave screens, the little holes? I used to work on the line that took those off the line after they were painted. You had to use these very heavy gloves because they were so hot. And we would take them off the line, and at the end of our shift, we’d have to take paper clips and poke through the holes if they were painted over.
**Sounds like a really creative job for you.**
I know, I kind of loved it. And then the one I worked at the longest, the factory that the one in the book is based on, it was a plastics factory. I was like [the character] Marcy, the white bumbling label operator. And then I got to move up to press operator, like Ada. So I’m very familiar with both their jobs, and it was just fun. I’ve always wanted to use that experience in a book because you just don’t read about it that often. It’s a fascinating setting because it’s dark, it’s at night, it’s in the middle of the woods, it’s very loud. So you can’t really hear anything but white noise. It has this creepiness to it that I love.

**Outside of those two points of view, you’ve interspersed shared Google doc entries, text exchanges, tweets, Facebook posts, and news reports. What was your thinking behind including those? Why that structure?**
Anytime I’m writing about a small town, there’s that claustrophobic, insular thing. But when it comes to an event, it wouldn’t make sense to me, it wouldn’t be as interesting, to just tell a story straight, like water-cooler talk. I don’t like it on TV or in books when someone says, “Well, so-and-so said this, and this, and this.” It feels like feeding information to the audience. It’s just not that dynamic. So with the interludes from the townspeople, I’ve got this kind of Greek chorus, little snippets of their perspective. It gives you a more well-rounded view of what it’s like in the town, what people are thinking and saying. And it gives you different demographics as well. It’s more storytelling, as opposed to writing. It’s way more fun. I [also] work a full-time day job in technology, and I don’t see anyone all day long. I’m always in Google, Google docs. I’m always on Slack and sending messages. I’m always texting. So [with] electronic communication —and the news, you know, news reports, Facebook, that sort of thing, Twitter— I’m just filling out the world.
**I’ve been thinking about the rate of revelation and how, in a good novel, the writer is constantly negotiating the questions she raises and the pace at which she answers them, if she answers them. Big questions obviously drive the plot (Whodunnit? Whodoinit?), and similar questions drive whole sections of the book (Where is Elijah? Will Ada and Nell get together?). But there are also more immediate scene-powering questions (Who or what made that noise?) and more overarching philosophical questions (Can love conquer loss?). I’m curious how consciously you managed all these question layers. What was your approach in creating the novel’s tension and momentum?**

I’m not the intellectual writer who thinks about all these things as I go along. I wish I could say I was. At the end of the day, I’m just trying to tell a good story. I’m not thinking about those little pieces. I’m literally just telling myself a story as I go, like, I’m my first reader. I also spend a ton of time daydreaming. In my head I’m editing, so by the time I put it on the page, it’s in pretty good shape. In many ways, it’s just based on intuition. Also reading across genre, outside of my own lane, is very helpful.
**What are you reading outside your own lane?**
Right now? Well, it’s still in my lane. I’m reading Megan Abbott’s _Beware the Woman_, which is amazing. I love her work. I want to be slotted next to her in terms of style because it’s a slow burn, and I love a slow burn. I want to take my time with sentences. I will read a page-turner, but for me, there’s nothing as satisfying as when you really get to appreciate the sentences and the tone and the atmosphere that a writer creates.
**Years ago you said you were drawn to “the intoxicating stew of shame, sexuality, Christianity, and crime.” Definitely those are in this novel, too, but so are guilt and abandonment and problematic or useless authority figures. What ideas powered this third novel, especially compared to your first two?**
I definitely didn’t start with theme. I think theme belongs to the reader. Because often I’m like, “Oh, I didn’t know that! That sounds cool.”
**If any part of the novel did not survive, why did you kill it?**
I cut about 50% to 75% of this. I was talking with my beta reader, and she was just like, “This feels like two different books.” And she was right. And so I was looking at it, and I was like, “Okay, so, I’ve got to take out _this_ book…” Luckily, that can be another book, right? So nothing is wasted. I use everything. But yeah, I had to rewrite everything new kind of late in the process. But it was fine because it worked out. I feel like I have a better book for it.

**In a 2017 interview for _Cottonmouths_, you said you’d love to see LGBTQ literature evolve to include more than the hurt, but first the rest of the world has to do its part in making a safe space for it. How do you think LGBTQ literature has evolved since then?**
There are definitely more books out there. There’s more awareness. There are more editors who are taking a chance on books by LGBTQ writers. Not _all_. We still hear things like, “I don’t know who this book would appeal to,” or “I’m not sure how wide a market there is for this.” I mean, all you have to do is open up Twitter to see that it’s not a great time for queer people. So there are always barriers. But a lot of queer people have come together. I can truly only talk about the crime fiction community, but I’m involved with the Queer Crime Writers group, and they’ve been instrumental. It’s wonderful as a writer to find people who you don’t have to explain anything to. Part of it is just finding your people and then supporting each other. Part of it is you don’t care anymore. If a straight person doesn’t get it, who cares? If you don’t want to read it, don’t read it.
**I really liked how you handled your characters. Because they’re all just people in the world, you know? The conflict in a novel with LGBTQ characters doesn’t always have to relate to identity politics. Just let me know them, and tell me a story.**
Yeah. And that’s what’s the most fun to do here. With this book, the characters are not struggling with their identity, but they’re struggling with a circumstance that puts them in a harrowing situation. And they just happen to be gay. But it’s also a critical piece of their identity because you just have a different lens when you’re not the same as everyone else.
**You’ve been navigating the publishing industry a while now. What have been your highs and lows?**

A high is right now. Writing can be heartbreaking and so beautiful and joyous. Publishing is primarily heartbreaking. Because it’s just a difficult industry. There are only so many editors. There’s only so much money that gets spread around to various authors. And so you’re shooting for the lottery. And it’s so tied to your identity, speaking of identity, that it’s crushing if you get a rejection. But I love where I’m at now. I love being a mid-career author, not because I’m so celebrated—most people have no idea who I am—but because I like being a part of a writer community that’s at the same level. It’s really fun. It’s nice to not feel that desperation.
When you’re an aspiring writer, you just have to live through it. It feels sometimes like there’s nothing that anyone, especially an established writer or a published writer, can tell you that can make you feel better. You’re just kind of like, “Well, that’s easy for you to say. You’re published.” Not feeling that anxiety anymore feels like such a gift. It took so much hard work to get there. But I’m grateful to be there, not because I have great success or anything, but because, you know, I’m just another writer out there doing my thing.
**If _The Hunt_ is your last book, will you be satisfied?**
Absolutely. Because when I write now, I feel that confidence and that comfort. I can just relax, and I feel like that shows in the writing. I feel like it’s expansive, and it can breathe a little bit. And that’s so much nicer than just agonizing over every sentence. Yeah, it’s more fun now. It’s a lot more fun now.

In the Arkansas of Kelly J. Ford’s third novel, _The Hunt_, Easter season does not mean pink bows and bunnies. It means bored or needy townspeople seeking a golden egg and prize money. Gossips and greedy sponsors seeking social currency and sales. Zealous Christians seeking recruits and redemption. Most of all, it means a disappearance and, usually, a death. Is there a seasonal serial killer on the loose? Will this year produce another victim?
Called “a modern master of the rural noir” and celebrated by Best Thriller Books for her “ability to draw readers into the chaos and craziness of everyday life while exploring themes of shared trauma, family dynamics, and the societal constraints of small-town America,” Kelly J. Ford has written her most multi-dimensional novel yet, introducing us to a compelling cast of characters whose humanity matters as much as their survival. What a treat to Zoom with her and learn about her fascinations, frustrations, and factory jobs on the way to her latest success.
**_The Hunt_****is populated with seekers, and you turn your readers into seekers, too. We _must_ figure out what’s going on in Presley. How much were you a seeker as you wrote the story? Did you know where it was headed?**
Whenever I’m writing, I’m always seeking because I never know the end. I feel like every draft, I’m just seeking the story. I have been using a lot of power tools lately that are breaking, and I have to take them apart. I’m like, “Well, you don’t know how to fix it until you take it apart.” So I try to apply that to revision. I’ll start a draft, and then I’ll go back through, and I’ll read it. And I’m like, “You know, this isn’t working. I need to fix this.” And so I kind of tear apart my drafts as I go. I might find something more interesting in a later draft and change my idea of what the ending is. The endings are so hard to land. You want something that’s resonant.
**Did you know if there was going to _be_ a hunter?**
texts.1:
I didn’t. I’m one of those readers who likes things a little bit ambiguous. I’m very much like a townsperson in the hunt: What _is_ going on? Who _is_ behind all of this? I start with this cast of characters, and I know how each of them ticks. For every single character, it’s like, What do they want? What is their obstacle? What are they going to do to get it? Once you have those kind of built-in engines, you can just let your plot go. And then it’s kind of fun. You go into that wonderful, trance-like state, and you start to figure it out, and then it’s almost like, “Oh, my God! _That’s_ what happened!”
**How did you determine the size of your character cast? Since everybody you introduce is a potential suspect or victim, I wondered if you felt your cast would get out of hand or if you felt, “No, it has to be this big.”**
This book is kind of the culmination of two other books that I trunked. I already had some characters that I really loved. I took two main characters that already existed from those books and put them into this book. And somehow, it worked. I knew I wanted Nell, and I knew I wanted Elijah, and they seemed like a perfect fit together: aunt and nephew bound by this circumstance of Elijah’s father going missing, and then his subsequent death, which many in town attribute to a serial killer. And when there’s a serial killer, you kind of don’t have a choice but to have a lot of characters. Inevitably, you have a giant cast.
texts.2:
But I also really love Jami Attenberg’s _The Middlesteins_. I love that book, and I was always like, “I would love to have a book that has all these characters and be able to see if I can do it.” The world of _Cottonmouths_, my debut, was so small—very few characters, very claustrophobic—and so it felt like a pressure cooker. And then _Real Bad Things_ was, again, not a ton of characters. So in a way, I just wanted to have fun and expand my cast. Then by nature of choosing Elijah… well, Elijah is 17 years old, so that [determined] a lot of the plotting. And not even plotting. More like logistics. Between me and my editor and my copy editor and the proofreader, we’re all like, “Wait a minute, what year is it?” We had all these lists written down, like, this is the year that this person died, and how they died…
**Why was Elijah so pivotal? It sounds as though you built your whole timeframe around him.**
Yeah, I just wanted to focus on the individuals impacted by these deaths. You know, thinking about things like true crime—the spectacle of true crime, but also the fascination with it—I mean, I’ll read a lot of that, but there is something icky about it at times. There are real people behind it. Elijah is pivotal in that it’s his father, it’s a loss, he never knew him, and there’s this entire event in town where everyone’s in a frenzy. And his father is the rumored first victim. That to me is so compelling, putting yourself into a person’s shoes. Our characters are people. They’re not just characters; they’re individuals that we live with for a long time. What must it be like for someone who has this hole in their heart? What must that feel like, especially when you never got to know them as a person and you can’t truly move on? Because there’s not real closure. I’m always fascinated by that angle of a crime. I’m just always fascinated with psychology. There are a lot of really excellent books that go into victim stories. So I wanted to bring that into it.
**For the most part, the novel tracks Nell and Ada using close third-person narration. Why did you decide to center both women’s experiences?**
texts.3:
They present two sides of the town. One side is like, “This hunt should not happen, even if there’s not a serial killer. There are deaths associated with it every year.” And this side is convinced it’s because of the hunt, serial killer or not. Nell, whose brother was affected, is more toward this side. But then on the other side, you’ve got people like Ada, who is an avid Egghead, someone who loves the hunt, who is more logical, thinking, “Of course people are going to get hurt. Nobody’s doing anything, and then suddenly everyone goes out and is active in the community, looking around, not paying attention, so you know, of course accidents happen.” I just wanted to have that closeness for both sides. I also wanted to present a different perspective on these working-class women in Arkansas. You don’t see that all the time, especially in Southern fiction, where the working class is often typical cisgender white males; they’re the ones working at the factories and having a hard time. So then it’s like, _I’ve_ worked in a factory, two factories in college.
**What did you do?**
Oh, my gosh. So the first one, you know microwave screens, the little holes? I used to work on the line that took those off the line after they were painted. You had to use these very heavy gloves because they were so hot. And we would take them off the line, and at the end of our shift, we’d have to take paper clips and poke through the holes if they were painted over.
**Sounds like a really creative job for you.**
I know, I kind of loved it. And then the one I worked at the longest, the factory that the one in the book is based on, it was a plastics factory. I was like [the character] Marcy, the white bumbling label operator. And then I got to move up to press operator, like Ada. So I’m very familiar with both their jobs, and it was just fun. I’ve always wanted to use that experience in a book because you just don’t read about it that often. It’s a fascinating setting because it’s dark, it’s at night, it’s in the middle of the woods, it’s very loud. So you can’t really hear anything but white noise. It has this creepiness to it that I love.
texts.4:
**Outside of those two points of view, you’ve interspersed shared Google doc entries, text exchanges, tweets, Facebook posts, and news reports. What was your thinking behind including those? Why that structure?**
Anytime I’m writing about a small town, there’s that claustrophobic, insular thing. But when it comes to an event, it wouldn’t make sense to me, it wouldn’t be as interesting, to just tell a story straight, like water-cooler talk. I don’t like it on TV or in books when someone says, “Well, so-and-so said this, and this, and this.” It feels like feeding information to the audience. It’s just not that dynamic. So with the interludes from the townspeople, I’ve got this kind of Greek chorus, little snippets of their perspective. It gives you a more well-rounded view of what it’s like in the town, what people are thinking and saying. And it gives you different demographics as well. It’s more storytelling, as opposed to writing. It’s way more fun. I [also] work a full-time day job in technology, and I don’t see anyone all day long. I’m always in Google, Google docs. I’m always on Slack and sending messages. I’m always texting. So [with] electronic communication —and the news, you know, news reports, Facebook, that sort of thing, Twitter— I’m just filling out the world.
**I’ve been thinking about the rate of revelation and how, in a good novel, the writer is constantly negotiating the questions she raises and the pace at which she answers them, if she answers them. Big questions obviously drive the plot (Whodunnit? Whodoinit?), and similar questions drive whole sections of the book (Where is Elijah? Will Ada and Nell get together?). But there are also more immediate scene-powering questions (Who or what made that noise?) and more overarching philosophical questions (Can love conquer loss?). I’m curious how consciously you managed all these question layers. What was your approach in creating the novel’s tension and momentum?**
texts.5:
I’m not the intellectual writer who thinks about all these things as I go along. I wish I could say I was. At the end of the day, I’m just trying to tell a good story. I’m not thinking about those little pieces. I’m literally just telling myself a story as I go, like, I’m my first reader. I also spend a ton of time daydreaming. In my head I’m editing, so by the time I put it on the page, it’s in pretty good shape. In many ways, it’s just based on intuition. Also reading across genre, outside of my own lane, is very helpful.
**What are you reading outside your own lane?**
Right now? Well, it’s still in my lane. I’m reading Megan Abbott’s _Beware the Woman_, which is amazing. I love her work. I want to be slotted next to her in terms of style because it’s a slow burn, and I love a slow burn. I want to take my time with sentences. I will read a page-turner, but for me, there’s nothing as satisfying as when you really get to appreciate the sentences and the tone and the atmosphere that a writer creates.
**Years ago you said you were drawn to “the intoxicating stew of shame, sexuality, Christianity, and crime.” Definitely those are in this novel, too, but so are guilt and abandonment and problematic or useless authority figures. What ideas powered this third novel, especially compared to your first two?**
I definitely didn’t start with theme. I think theme belongs to the reader. Because often I’m like, “Oh, I didn’t know that! That sounds cool.”
**If any part of the novel did not survive, why did you kill it?**
I cut about 50% to 75% of this. I was talking with my beta reader, and she was just like, “This feels like two different books.” And she was right. And so I was looking at it, and I was like, “Okay, so, I’ve got to take out _this_ book…” Luckily, that can be another book, right? So nothing is wasted. I use everything. But yeah, I had to rewrite everything new kind of late in the process. But it was fine because it worked out. I feel like I have a better book for it.
texts.6:
**In a 2017 interview for _Cottonmouths_, you said you’d love to see LGBTQ literature evolve to include more than the hurt, but first the rest of the world has to do its part in making a safe space for it. How do you think LGBTQ literature has evolved since then?**
There are definitely more books out there. There’s more awareness. There are more editors who are taking a chance on books by LGBTQ writers. Not _all_. We still hear things like, “I don’t know who this book would appeal to,” or “I’m not sure how wide a market there is for this.” I mean, all you have to do is open up Twitter to see that it’s not a great time for queer people. So there are always barriers. But a lot of queer people have come together. I can truly only talk about the crime fiction community, but I’m involved with the Queer Crime Writers group, and they’ve been instrumental. It’s wonderful as a writer to find people who you don’t have to explain anything to. Part of it is just finding your people and then supporting each other. Part of it is you don’t care anymore. If a straight person doesn’t get it, who cares? If you don’t want to read it, don’t read it.
**I really liked how you handled your characters. Because they’re all just people in the world, you know? The conflict in a novel with LGBTQ characters doesn’t always have to relate to identity politics. Just let me know them, and tell me a story.**
Yeah. And that’s what’s the most fun to do here. With this book, the characters are not struggling with their identity, but they’re struggling with a circumstance that puts them in a harrowing situation. And they just happen to be gay. But it’s also a critical piece of their identity because you just have a different lens when you’re not the same as everyone else.
**You’ve been navigating the publishing industry a while now. What have been your highs and lows?**
texts.7:
A high is right now. Writing can be heartbreaking and so beautiful and joyous. Publishing is primarily heartbreaking. Because it’s just a difficult industry. There are only so many editors. There’s only so much money that gets spread around to various authors. And so you’re shooting for the lottery. And it’s so tied to your identity, speaking of identity, that it’s crushing if you get a rejection. But I love where I’m at now. I love being a mid-career author, not because I’m so celebrated—most people have no idea who I am—but because I like being a part of a writer community that’s at the same level. It’s really fun. It’s nice to not feel that desperation.
When you’re an aspiring writer, you just have to live through it. It feels sometimes like there’s nothing that anyone, especially an established writer or a published writer, can tell you that can make you feel better. You’re just kind of like, “Well, that’s easy for you to say. You’re published.” Not feeling that anxiety anymore feels like such a gift. It took so much hard work to get there. But I’m grateful to be there, not because I have great success or anything, but because, you know, I’m just another writer out there doing my thing.
**If _The Hunt_ is your last book, will you be satisfied?**
Absolutely. Because when I write now, I feel that confidence and that comfort. I can just relax, and I feel like that shows in the writing. I feel like it’s expansive, and it can breathe a little bit. And that’s so much nicer than just agonizing over every sentence. Yeah, it’s more fun now. It’s a lot more fun now.

# Scholarly association backs Indigenous author award
The Emerging Indigenous Voices Awards will help support the work of young Indigenous writers.
By
Melanie Lefebvre
August 29, 2017
Posted in

0 Comments
This fall, the Indigenous Literary Studies Association will reveal the details of its inaugural literary award, a prize that started as a grassroots show of support for young Indigenous writers.
The award can be traced back to May 2017 when _Write_ magazine ran an editorial encouraging the appropriation of Indigenous experience in literature, in a special issue of the publication that had focused on the work of Indigenous authors. The fallout shone a spotlight on the lack of representation of Indigenous people, Black people and people of colour in Canadian media, and inspired a collective response of outrage and action. Toronto lawyer Robin Parker and Vancouver writer Silvia Moreno-Garcia spearheaded a crowdfunding campaign to support the Indigenous writers at the heart of the controversy.
Funds and support poured in – now at over $116,000 – and the initiative was championed as the Emerging Indigenous Voices Awards. With a focus on sustainable funding, organizers are seeking to raise a total of $150,000 and have tasked administration and distribution of the prize to ILSA, a scholarly body created in 2013.
“ILSA is working with several universities to find the right vehicle to distribute the funds to ensure ethical distribution,” says Deanna Reder, president of ILSA and a professor at Simon Fraser University.
The first jury includes Kateri Akiwenzie-Damm, an Anishnaabe writer and publisher of mixed ancestry from the Chippewas of Nawash First Nation; Canadian broadcast journalist, Shelagh Rogers; Haitian-Canadian francophone poet Rodney Saint-Éloi; Red River Métis writer and teacher Gregory Scofield; Tlicho and Dene author Richard Van Camp from Fort Smith, Northwest Territories.

# Scholarly association backs Indigenous author award
In his forthcoming book _Why Indigenous Literatures Matter_, Cherokee Nation academic and author Daniel Heath Justice, who worked closely with ILSA to establish the award, affirms the relationship between Indigenous literature, experience and traditions: “By centring voices, perspectives, and subjectivities too often pushed to the margins, we might better understand where we’ve come from, where we are in the world today, and how we might realize better ways of being in the future.”
Winners of the Emerging Indigenous Voice Awards are expected to be announced at the 2018 ILSA conference.

Barnes said books are a big part of his household, and he often talks about the importance of reading as he travels. He also said he tries to center “the humanity and brilliance and beauty of black children” in his work.
The gathering is also tied to an inaugural literary award honoring Janice Barbara Wilson, an educator and librarian in Little Rock who died earlier this year. Oliver said Wilson helped shape how he works with children and previously hosted Barnes during what he believes was Barnes’ first visit to Arkansas.

# Scholarly association backs Indigenous author award
The Emerging Indigenous Voices Awards will help support the work of young Indigenous writers.
By
Melanie Lefebvre
August 29, 2017
Posted in

0 Comments
This fall, the Indigenous Literary Studies Association will reveal the details of its inaugural literary award, a prize that started as a grassroots show of support for young Indigenous writers.
The award can be traced back to May 2017 when _Write_ magazine ran an editorial encouraging the appropriation of Indigenous experience in literature, in a special issue of the publication that had focused on the work of Indigenous authors. The fallout shone a spotlight on the lack of representation of Indigenous people, Black people and people of colour in Canadian media, and inspired a collective response of outrage and action. Toronto lawyer Robin Parker and Vancouver writer Silvia Moreno-Garcia spearheaded a crowdfunding campaign to support the Indigenous writers at the heart of the controversy.
Funds and support poured in – now at over $116,000 – and the initiative was championed as the Emerging Indigenous Voices Awards. With a focus on sustainable funding, organizers are seeking to raise a total of $150,000 and have tasked administration and distribution of the prize to ILSA, a scholarly body created in 2013.
“ILSA is working with several universities to find the right vehicle to distribute the funds to ensure ethical distribution,” says Deanna Reder, president of ILSA and a professor at Simon Fraser University.
The first jury includes Kateri Akiwenzie-Damm, an Anishnaabe writer and publisher of mixed ancestry from the Chippewas of Nawash First Nation; Canadian broadcast journalist, Shelagh Rogers; Haitian-Canadian francophone poet Rodney Saint-Éloi; Red River Métis writer and teacher Gregory Scofield; Tlicho and Dene author Richard Van Camp from Fort Smith, Northwest Territories.

Winners of the Emerging Indigenous Voice Awards are expected to be announced at the 2018 ILSA conference.
